summary: Deprecates the IPv6 Type 0 Routing Header because it can be abused to amplify traffic along a remote path for denial-of-service attacks. It updates the IPv6 specification. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A feature let one sender make a packet bounce back and forth along a path, flooding it. This tells everyone to stop using the feature.

questions: why was ipv6 type 0 routing header deprecated
what is the ipv6 type 0 routing header
how does an rh0 amplification attack work
subtitle: Why IPv6 nodes were told to stop processing Type 0 Routing Headers.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 Type 0 Routing Header (RH0) lets an attacker list the same intermediate addresses many times, so packets bounce between two remote nodes and amplify traffic along the path between them.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes MUST NOT run the RH0 algorithm and instead treat RH0 like an unrecognised Routing Type; operators are told to use ingress filtering and to block only Type 0, not all Routing Headers.
tldr.outcome: RH0 is deprecated and implementations no longer need to support it. It updates RFC 2460 and RFC 4294.

today: RFC 5095 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2460 and RFC 4294, so RH0 is deprecated.

sections.title: The Problem With RH0
sections.content:
RFC 2460 defines the IPv6 Routing Header, an extension header identified by a Next Header value of 43. One subtype, Type 0, is called RH0 here.

A single RH0 may hold many intermediate node addresses, and the same address may appear more than once. A packet can therefore be built to oscillate between two RH0-processing hosts or routers many times. A stream of attacker packets is amplified along the path between those two remote routers, which can cause congestion on arbitrary remote paths and so act as a denial-of-service mechanism. An 88-fold amplification has been demonstrated.

The attack affects the entire path between the two exploited nodes, not only the nodes or their local networks. The IPv4 source route option has similar functionality, but RH0 allows many more intermediate addresses per packet.
sections.eli5: Imagine writing a delivery route that sends a parcel back and forth between two shops hundreds of times. All the trucks in between get jammed.

sections.title: How the Risk Was Found
sections.content:
Problems with RH0 were identified in 2001, and a 2002 proposal suggested restricting Routing Header processing in hosts. These efforts led Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) to use the type 2 Routing Header instead of RH0.

In 2006 Vishwas Manral identified several risks, including the amplification attack, and some were later documented in RFC 4942. A 2007 talk at the CanSecWest conference gave the risks widespread publicity.

The authors judge the threat serious enough to deprecate RH0 entirely. A side effect is that benign uses of RH0 disappear too, though future Routing Header specifications may serve them.
sections.eli5: People noticed the trick one by one over several years, until a conference talk made everyone pay attention.

sections.title: Deprecation of RH0
sections.content:
An IPv6 node that receives a packet addressed to it and containing an RH0 MUST NOT execute the RH0 algorithm from section 4.4 of RFC 2460. Instead, the packet MUST be handled as a datagram with an unrecognised Routing Type value.

  • If Segments Left is zero, the node ignores the Routing header and processes the next header.
  • If Segments Left is non-zero, the node discards the packet and sends an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 0, message to the packet's Source Address, pointing to the unrecognized Routing Type.

IPv6 implementations are no longer required to implement RH0 in any way.
sections.eli5: If a packet arrives with the bouncing route, the computer acts as if it has never heard of that kind of route. It either skips it or throws the packet away and tells the sender.

sections.title: Operational Advice
sections.content:
Not all IPv6 nodes will be updated at once. Some RH0 uses can be mitigated with ingress filtering, as recommended in RFC 2827 and RFC 3704. A site security policy meant to protect against RH0 attacks SHOULD include ingress filtering at the site border.

Firewalls must be careful. Blocking all packets with any Routing Header has serious implications for IPv6 development: if even a small percentage of firewalls block other types by default, extending Routing Headers becomes impossible in practice. Mobile IPv6 relies on a Type 2 Routing Header and would become undeployable.

So firewall policy against RH0 MUST NOT simply filter all traffic with a Routing Header. It must be possible to disable forwarding of Type 0 traffic without blocking other types, and the default configuration MUST permit forwarding of Routing Headers other than 0.
sections.eli5: Block only the bad kind of route. If you shut out every kind of route, good ones can never be used either.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The whole document exists to deprecate a feature shown to have undesirable security implications. RH0 gives a mechanism for traffic amplification that might be used as a denial-of-service attack. Specific vulnerabilities are described in the CanSecWest presentation.

For IANA, the registry "Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Parameters" should be updated to show that variant 0 of IPv6 header-type 43 ("Routing Header") is deprecated.
sections.eli5: The fix is to remove the risky feature, and the official list of header types gets a note saying it is retired.
